zones.note: The scan actually prints S ANTES DO V. above this T-section page. The anomalous running header is preserved, not corrected to match the contents.

zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical aid (consulted after independent scan reading): NINJAL, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, supplied page subset, CC BY 4.0. Source: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . Its headwords and derived kana do not establish this copy’s spelling or typography; the transcription follows the supplied BnF native scan.

runs.text: reuela o Cami entrando no corpo dalguem.

lines.note: Continues a prior definition about a kami revealing something by entering a person’s body. This is a page-top continuation, not the end of f462’s falcon entry; intervening original leaves are absent from the supplied sequence.
Takushi concerns possession: a kami enters or inhabits someone. The scan shows initial T, correcting OCR Facuxi; the Portuguese sentence continues below.
Adds “or the devil, in someone.” These are the dictionary’s explanatory categories for the possession verb, not separate headwords.

Tada is labelled adverbial and glossed with “only,” mas, and aßi. The following example begins tadano koto dewa nai; the printed gloss is retained without replacing mas from modern expectations. The separate second pass and enlargement show a grave accent in Sòmente; it is retained rather than normalized to somente.
Completes tadano koto dewa nai, “it is no ordinary matter.” The Portuguese qualquer couſa is divided across this row and the next.
After completing cousa, tada maitta illustrates arriving empty-handed or for no particular cause. Na- begins nada in the translation.
Completes “came without bringing anything, or came without a reason.” The two readings explicate the preceding tada example.
Tadabashiri means running at full speed. Tadabaxi- begins the adverbial example continued below.
Rini completes tadabashirini; with hashiru it means running flat out. The Portuguese reiterates “go at a full run.”
Tadabito is equated with bonnin, an ordinary person. The Portuguese qualification continues to distinguish learning and rank.
The ordinary person is described as lacking learning or social dignity. This is the historical dictionary’s characterization, not a new moral judgment.
Tadachini here means directly or face to face. The next row completes the repeated rosto phrase; the sense is not limited to modern “immediately.”
Tadachini ōse tsukeraruru illustrates a lord issuing an order directly. The printed vôxe bears an upward circumflex.

runs.text: Mandar o ſenhor algũa couſa rectamẽ-

lines.note: Ru completes the honorific verb. The Portuguese describes the lord giving an order directly, with rectamẽte split across the row boundary.
Completes “directly, or in person.” This clarifies that the example concerns personal delivery of an order.
Tadacoto, explained as tadano coto, means an ordinary matter. The divided Portuguese ordinaria continues below.

runs.text: ria, ou cõmuã: ſempre ſe ajunta com negatiuo.

lines.note: Completes “ordinary or common” and says the expression is used with a negative. Both printed nasal marks in cõmuã are retained.
Tadacoto dewa nai illustrates “this is no ordinary thing.” The Portuguese qual continues as quer without adding a hyphen absent from the scan.
Completes “any thing, or one of the ordinary ones.” This belongs to the negative example, not a separate definition.
Tadacuchi concerns a mouth that is never idle. The first example describes a person who is constantly speaking or eating, as the following translation explains.

runs.text: l, Tadacuchimonǒ yǔ. l, cù fitode go-

lines.note: Alternative formulations use yǔ, speaking, and cù, eating. The printed long-vowel marks and attached Tadacuchimonǒ are preserved rather than recast into modern spelling.

runs.text: He homem que de contino fala, ou

lines.note: Zaru completes gozaru. The Portuguese begins “a person who continually speaks, or…,” continuing with eating below.

runs.text: come, ou não eſtà ocioſo com a lingua.

lines.note: Completes the alternatives: eating, or not leaving the tongue idle. The first come is slightly damaged but remains readable in this coordinated sentence.

runs.text: Tadagauo. l, Sugauo. i, Qexǒmo nai cauo.

lines.note: Tadagao, alternatively sugao, is explained as a face without cosmetic adornment. Qexǒmo nai cauo supplies that Japanese paraphrase.
The Portuguese describes a face without applied cosmetics or embellishment. Posturas here belongs to facial adornment, not bodily posture.
Tadagashi is lending without taking interest, explained by ri wo toraide kasu. Empreſti- begins the Portuguese noun completed below.
Completes empréstimo: a loan without interest or gain. The historical term onzena and abbreviated nẽ are retained.
Tadagoi means asking insistently or importunately. The following example repeats the noun in an adverbial phrase.
Tadagoini kō is asking in that insistent manner; Idem sends the reader back to the preceding gloss. Cô has a clear circumflex.
Tadajime means pressing or tightening strongly. The headword’s m is weak but agrees with the clearly repeated Tadajime- on the same row, correcting OCR Tadajine.
Ni shimuru completes the repeated phrase. The Portuguese says the person did nothing but tighten or press, preserving the printed tense of its paraphrase.
Tadaima means just now or a moment ago. Ainda agora is the direct Portuguese adverbial gloss.

runs.text: Xiro frio feito concerta erua que

lines.note: Tadamijiru denotes a cold soup prepared with the herb tade and miso, as the next row specifies. The headword’s m is abraded and its separated strokes can resemble ni; Tadamijiru is the usable reading adopted, supported but not proved by the supplied NINJAL entry. Printed Xiro and the close setting concerta are preserved.

runs.text: chamão Tade, & Miſo ſem ſe cozer.

lines.note: The herb is called Tade, and miso is added without cooking. Tade and Miſo are Japanese food terms embedded in the Portuguese definition; no modern recipe is supplied.

runs.text: Parte do corpo a baixo dos peitos.

lines.note: Tadanaca first names the body region below the chest. Its figurative use follows on the next row.
Restores the visible paragraph mark before the figurative label. Tadanaka wo yū, or mat-tadanaka wo yū, concerns speaking to the very point of a matter; the latter phrase is physically divided.

runs.text: Dar no aluo da couſa, ou a-

lines.note: Danacauo completes the second phrase. The final verb is yǔ, not OCR yǒ; the Portuguese gloss means hitting the point or target of the matter.

runs.text: certar no intimo da verdade, razão, &c.

lines.note: Completes acertar: reaching the heart of truth or reason. This is the figurative application of the body-centre expression.

Tadano is labelled adjectival and referred back to Tada. Enlargement shows Adiect. with an i and the ct ligature, not Adiest. or Adject.; the cross-reference Tada is itself in italic type within the Portuguese apparatus.
Tadaracaxi is described as a verb commonly combined with others. Its function is explained through scratching, writing and chewing examples rather than a single isolated translation.

runs.text: mente ſe vſa junto aoutros. Vt,

lines.note: Completes “commonly used together with others” and begins kaki-tadarakasu. The example’s final caſu continues on the next physical row.
Caſu completes the compound: scratching a scabby or itchy area excessively. The Portuguese dei- continues as deixandoa below.
Completes the result of scratching: leaving it injured and bloody. Enſangoentada is retained as printed rather than regularized to a modern spelling.
A further figurative application describes writing by scratching and blotting. Bor- begins borrando across the row boundary.
Completes borrando, then gives kami-tadarakasu, chewing badly. Cami here is the verb stem “chew,” not the deity noun seen at the top of the page.

runs.text: mal, ficando o comer engorlado, como fazem os

lines.note: The food is left lumpy or poorly chewed. Engorlado is the printed descriptive word; the comparison with toothless old people continues below. The comma after engorlado is visible on the second scan pass.

runs.text: velhos que nao tem dentes: & aßi junto com

lines.note: Completes the comparison with people lacking teeth, then resumes the rule about combination with other verbs in column 2. The printed nao has no securely visible tilde.

runs.text: outros verbos na raiz ſignifica fazer mal, ou

lines.note: Continues the general rule: attached to other verb stems, tadarakasu means doing their action badly or damaging something. The following row supplies the final object.
Completes the preceding compound-verb rule with “damage something.” This remains part of tadaracaxi before the new tadare entry.
Tadare describes the condition of an ulcer or wound. The Portuguese predicate continues below with poorly healed edges and inflammation.
The wound has poorly healed, festering edges. Me ga begins the next example about the eyes; it is not part of the Portuguese sentence.
Me ga tadaruru describes inflamed eyes. The Portuguese first calls them red, adding their discharge on the following row.
Completes “red and rheumy,” then gives kasa ga tadarete aru for an inflamed skin eruption. Eſ- begins its Portuguese translation.
Completes “the eruption is inflamed,” then starts kirime ga tadaruru. This shifts from inflamed tissue to a badly made cut.

runs.text: Eſtar a couſa mal cortada, & de-

lines.note: Daruru completes the verb; the Portuguese explains an object cut badly and unevenly. De- continues as desigualmente below.

runs.text: ſigualmente, como cortada com ferro que corta

lines.note: Completes desigualmente and compares the result to a cut made with an ineffective blade. The comparison continues on the next row.
Completes “with an iron that cuts badly, or with a saw.” The rough-cut comparison closes the tadare entry.
Tadarecacari means being importunate or tiresome. The following lines specify persistent requests and creating difficulties.

runs.text: prolixo com pedir algũa couſa, ou com aleuan-

lines.note: The person is tedious through repeatedly asking for something or raising a difficulty. Aleuan- is physically divided before tar.
Completes levantar algum caramilho: stirring up a troublesome affair or obstruction. The paired embaraço supports that contextual meaning rather than the musical sense of a similar-looking word.
Tadaremono labels the corresponding tiresome person. The following description develops their involvement in troubles and obstructions.
Completes the description as a person of tricks, disputes or encumbrances. It is attached to tadaremono, not the next eye-condition noun.
Tadareme means rheumy or inflamed eyes. The short Portuguese gloss repeats the eye sense illustrated under tadare.
Tadasaqi denotes the falcon’s left side. Aparte retains the print’s close setting; the following example specifies its left wing.
Tadasaqino fa means the left wing of the falcon. Fa is the historical wing word; the gloss is unambiguous.
Miyori names the corresponding right side or wing. The paragraph sign is clearly present and has been restored.
Tadaxi is the adversative or qualifying expression “except that / however.” The compact Saluoſe is retained as printed rather than silently spaced into modern Portuguese.
The verb tadaxi, tadasu, tadaita means investigating or judging. Its printed historical past form aita is retained.
Restores the paragraph sign before sujime wo tadasu. The gloss begins finding the thread or line, continued into an explanation of disentangling it.

runs.text: nha que està embaraçada, & pola em ſeu lu-

lines.note: Nha completes linha: a tangled thread is found and put in its proper place. Lu- continues as lugar below.

runs.text: gar. ¶ Item, per met. Inquirir a gèração,

lines.note: Gar completes lugar. The figurative extension is to investigate someone’s descent or lineage. The small dot-like mark above the e of gèração is retained provisionally as the draft’s grave accent; its exact graphic shape remains uncertain at enlargement.
Ou linhagẽ dalguem completes “or someone’s lineage.” This reinforces the genealogical sense rather than general questioning.
Tadashifuse means reaching a final judgment. Vltimamen- is the beginning of the Portuguese adverb continued below.
Completes “judge finally, or deliver a sentence.” This is the concluding-decision sense of the compound verb.
Tadaxij means upright, just or faithful. The Ta- at the right begins the example of an upright person.
Daxij fito completes tadashii hito, an upright and faithful person. The translation directly illustrates the adjective.
Tadaxiſa is the corresponding abstract noun, uprightness or correctness. It is printed alone on its own indented physical row.
Tadaxǔ is the adverbial form belonging to tadashii. The caron is over u, not o; no additional Portuguese gloss is printed on this row.
Tadaxite names a judge or one who judges. Iuiz preserves the historical initial I rather than modern J.

Tadayoi describes a vessel rocking on the water; both o marks point upward. The second pass resolves the word boundary Andar a, while the line ends in balã, continued by ceandoſe below; no unprinted terminal hyphen is supplied.

runs.text: ceandoſe na agoa, ou andar ao pairo. Item,

lines.note: Ceandoſe completes the rocking verb, followed by the nautical phrase andar ao pairo. The gloss covers a boat lying or moving idly on the water.

runs.text: Andar cabeceando como velhos, ou bebados,

lines.note: Another sense concerns moving with a nodding or swaying head, compared here with elderly or drunken people. The next example illustrates unstable walking.
Ashi ga tadayōte yuku describes walking with wavering steps. The Portuguese starts “the drunk person goes…,” completed below.
Completes the staggering example, then introduces hanukedori, birds whose flight feathers have been lost. The wave-related predicate follows on the next line.
Nami ni tadayō describes the birds drifting on waves. The Portuguese begins an explanation involving certain water birds.

runs.text: dagoa como marrecas deſaſados, ou ſem penas

lines.note: The birds are compared with teal or ducks lacking their wing feathers. The print says deſaſados; it is not normalized from the expected feather-loss description.

runs.text: nas aſas às voltas com as ondas.

lines.note: Completes the image of the featherless-winged birds moving about with the waves. The prepositional phrase belongs to the drifting example.
Tadayoiaruki is referred back to the wavering movement sense. Fito- starts the example of a person wandering.
Hito ga tadayoiariku means a person wandering without a settled place. The printed ariqu in the example differs from aruqi in the headword and is preserved.

runs.text: terrado ſem caſa, & lugar certo decà pera là.

lines.note: Completes the comparison with an exile who has neither house nor fixed place, wandering here and there. Decà retains its printed close setting and grave.

runs.text: Hũa erua que requeima de que ſe faz

lines.note: Tade is a pungent herb used in a sauce. The opening letter is T, not OCR F; the wording does not require a species identification.
Completes “a kind of sauce.” This closes the plant noun, distinct from the following verb of treatment.
The verb tade describes washing an itchy eruption and patting it with something. The scan has initial T and the printed principal form zzuru.

runs.text: algum pano pera mitigar a dor, ou coceira.

lines.note: A cloth is used to relieve pain or itching, according to the historical gloss. The entry continues on f464 after the repeated catchword; this is transcription of the source, not treatment advice.

zones.label: Printed catchword
zones.note: This catchword is repeated at the opening of f464.
